title: Providing Context to the Maths We Teach
author: Harry Zafar
summary: Harry Zafar argues that many mathematical conventions reach students as arbitrary rules, which leads some to switch off and others to treat maths as a set of procedures to memorise. His remedy is to open a topic with a short story of where the idea came from, such as why a full turn is 360 degrees, why algebra uses letters, or how Egyptian rope stretchers made right angles. He then refers back to that context when the procedure arrives, so the protractor or the algebraic expression has a reason behind it. He builds the stories from his own knowledge and research and uses Gemini to interrogate a topic, noting that AI only produces a good narrative when the teacher prompts it with a clear aim. The idea extends to other topics such as the history of metric and imperial units.
points: Unexplained conventions teach students that maths is a set of rules that simply is, which pushes some away and leaves others with procedures only.
Beginning a unit with a short historical story, such as the Babylonian 360-degree circle, gives angle measurement a reason before the procedure.
Referring back to the story during the maths makes a half turn of 180 degrees meaningful rather than a fact to recall.
AI is useful for building such stories only when the teacher supplies a clear aim and key developments to include.
quotes: My thought is that if we dive straight into measuring angles, writing algebraic expressions, or working with coordinates, students often either switch off or see these important concepts as rules or processes to remember rather than as important and useful ideas. For some students, this is fine for ‘learning’ maths, but for most, it makes the subject difficult to grasp and enjoy.

More than this, I feel that it tells students that Maths is a set of rules to learn, or that it is something that ‘just is’. Angles around a point sum to 360 because they just do. ‘x’ represents an unknown because it just does, and always has.

Instead, how about we start a Year 7 unit on angles by talking about how, if you stand in a spot and turn all the way back to where you started, that is a full turn. We know a full turn is 360 degrees from primary school, but why?
They called the unknown value shay (Arabic for “thing”). Imagine doing your homework if every single problem was a paragraph! This is what we call Rhetorical Algebra.
It takes away the idea that measuring an angle is just a “procedure” to follow. It helps students understand that a “half turn” is 180 degrees within this context.

I generally use facts I have picked up and interrogate Gemini to gain a picture of a topic, if I want to present this kind of thing to students. AI generally doesn’t provide a well-structured, fully informed story without prompting you for what you want. E.g. what key developments do you want to include, what is the aim of your story? It’s definitely worth playing around with, if you are at all interested.
